messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: autocorrelation plots
parts:
This is a mix of a simple question about rstan and a less simple
question of diagnostics.

It doesn't look as if rstan provides a way to graph the autocorrelations
over different lags. Am I missing something?

If it's missing, is it missing because of doubts about the utility of
such plots? My interest is in figuring how much thinning to do to get
it down to a "reasonable" level.

R already has other tools that can generate such plots for suitably
extracted coefficient values. Of course, I have many chains and many
coefficients, which is perhaps one clue why the feature isn't there.
But I could identify the coefficient with the lowest n_eff and then look
at the plot for it.

My runs are currently sized to keep the minimum n_eff over 100. But
doubts about effective sample size for our final results (topic of my
previous post--thanks, Bob for the response) have led to an interest in
stretching out the chains to reduce the autocorrelations.

Originally I thought estimating the models would be slow but doing
simulations with them to estimate effects would be quick. It turns out
the reverse is true, and so longer estimation runs aren't looking so bad
now.

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autocorrelation plots
parts:
Check out the ggmcmc package, specifically:

    ggmcmc( ggs( stanOut ) , file=NULL, plot="ggs_autocorrelation")

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autocorrelation plots
parts:
In most cases you should never need to look at the autocorrelation plots as the relevant info is incorporate into N_eff which is available
through all of the interfaces.  For example, if you generate 1000 samples but see N_eff = 100 then the natural thinning is 10.

As Mike notes thinning is a wasteful as you are literally throwing information away.  Geyer has a nice discussion in the Handbook of
MCMC (conveniently available for free, http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf); he's an advocate of batches where
you average over a bin instead of taking a single sample.  Of course the problem there is that you're then stuck with the parameterization
of the chain and cannot compute the expectations of any nonlinear functions.

In the end thinning should be reserved for when you really do have huge autocorrelations and the output size becomes unmanageable
and only then.
